title: Java
summary: Learn Java from your first public class Main to interfaces, generics, collections and streams. Every lesson has a narrated video, notes, a quiz and a judged coding exercise.

lessons.title: Your first Java program
lessons.summary: Write, compile and run a Java program with a main method and System.out.println.

slides.title: What is Java?
slides.text:
Java is a **compiled**, **object-oriented** language used for Android apps, servers and big business systems.

- Write `.java` source
- Compile to bytecode
- The JVM runs it anywhere
slides.narration: Java is one of the most widely used languages in the world. You write source code, the compiler turns it into bytecode, and the Java Virtual Machine runs that bytecode on any computer. Write once, run anywhere.

slides.title: The smallest program
slides.text: Every Java program lives in a **class**. Execution starts in `main`.
slides.narration: Java is strict about structure. All code lives inside a class, and the program starts in a special method called main. In this editor, your class is always called Main.

slides.title: println vs print
slides.text:
- `System.out.println(x)` prints and moves to a new line
- `System.out.print(x)` stays on the same line
slides.narration: To show text you use System dot out dot println. The l n at the end means line: it adds a new line after the text. Plain print does not, so the next output continues on the same line.

slides.title: Semicolons and braces
slides.text:
- Every statement ends with `;`
- Curly braces `{ }` group code into blocks
- Java is **case sensitive**
slides.narration: Every instruction in Java ends with a semicolon, and curly braces mark where blocks begin and end. Capital letters matter, so System with a capital S is not the same as system.

slides.title: Comments
slides.text: `// one line` and `/* several lines */` are ignored by the compiler.
slides.narration: Comments are notes for people. Two slashes start a comment until the end of the line. Slash star starts a comment that can span several lines and ends with star slash.

lessons.notes:
## The structure of a Java program

```java
public class Main {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hello, world!");
    }
}
```

- `public class Main` declares a class named `Main`. The file must be called `Main.java`.
- `public static void main(String[] args)` is the **entry point**. The JVM calls it first.
- `System.out.println(...)` prints a line.

## Compile and run

Outside this editor you would type:

```
javac Main.java   # compile to Main.class
java Main         # run it
```

The editor does both steps for you when you press Run.

## Printing

```java
System.out.println("Text");       // with newline
System.out.print("No newline");   // without
System.out.println("Sum: " + (2 + 3));
```

Strings use **double quotes**. The `+` operator joins strings with other values. Use brackets when you want math to happen first: `"Sum: " + 2 + 3` gives `Sum: 23`, but `"Sum: " + (2 + 3)` gives `Sum: 5`.

## Common mistakes

- Missing semicolon: `error: ';' expected`.
- Class name different from file name.
- Writing `system.out.println` in lowercase.
- Unbalanced braces. Indent your code so each `{` lines up with its `}`.

Compiler errors are your friend: they show the line number and what Java expected.

quiz.q: Where does a Java program start running?
options: The first line of the file
quiz.explain: The JVM calls public static void main(String[] args) first.

quiz.q: What is the difference between print and println?
options: println adds a new line at the end
quiz.explain: println moves to a new line after printing.

quiz.q: What does System.out.println("A" + 1 + 2) print?
quiz.explain: Left to right: "A" + 1 is "A1", then + 2 gives "A12".

exercise.title: Say hello
exercise.prompt:
Read a **name** (one line) from standard input and print exactly:

```
Hello, NAME!
```

Use a `Scanner` with `nextLine()` (already set up in the starter).

lessons.title: Variables and types
lessons.summary: Declare typed variables, use primitive types and do arithmetic.

slides.title: Typed boxes
slides.text:
In Java every variable has a **fixed type** you declare first.

`int age = 15;`
slides.narration: Java is statically typed. When you create a variable you say what type it holds, and it can never hold a different type. The compiler checks this before the program runs, which catches many mistakes early.

slides.title: Primitive types
slides.text:
- `int` whole numbers
- `long` big whole numbers
- `double` decimals
- `boolean` true/false
- `char` one character
slides.narration: Java has eight primitive types. The ones you will use most are int for whole numbers, long for very big ones, double for decimals, boolean for true or false, and char for a single character in single quotes.

slides.title: Arithmetic
slides.text: `+ - * / %` work as usual. **int / int gives an int**: `7 / 2` is `3`.
slides.code:
System.out.println(7 / 2);      // 3
System.out.println(7 / 2.0);    // 3.5
System.out.println(7 % 2);      // 1
System.out.println((double) 7 / 2);
slides.narration: Be careful with division. When both sides are integers, Java throws away the decimal part. If you want three point five, make at least one side a double.

slides.title: var and final
slides.text:
- `var x = 5;` lets Java infer the type
- `final` makes a variable constant
slides.narration: Modern Java lets you write var for local variables, and the compiler works out the type from the value. The keyword final means the value can never change, which is perfect for constants.

slides.title: Overflow and casting
slides.text: An `int` holds up to about **2.1 billion**. Use `long` for bigger results. Cast with `(int)`, `(double)`.
slides.narration: Every number type has limits. If an int grows past about two billion it wraps around to a negative number, which is called overflow. Use long for big values, and use a cast to convert between number types.

lessons.notes:
## Declaring variables

```java
int score = 0;
double average = 7.5;
char grade = 'A';
boolean passed = true;
String city = "Lima";      // String is a class, not a primitive
```

Once declared, a variable keeps its type: `score = "ten";` is a compile error.

## Primitive types

| Type | Size | Example |
|------|------|---------|
| `byte` | 8 bit | `100` |
| `short` | 16 bit | `30000` |
| `int` | 32 bit | `2_000_000` |
| `long` | 64 bit | `9_000_000_000L` |
| `float` | 32 bit | `1.5f` |
| `double` | 64 bit | `3.14` |
| `char` | 16 bit | `'x'` |
| `boolean` | - | `true` |

## Operators

```java
int a = 17, b = 5;
a + b;   // 22
a / b;   // 3   (integer division)
a % b;   // 2   (remainder)
a += 3;  // a is now 20
a++;     // a is now 21
```

## Casting

```java
double d = 9.7;
int i = (int) d;         // 9, decimals cut off
double avg = (double) 7 / 2;   // 3.5
long big = 3_000_000_000L;
```

## Math helpers

```java
Math.max(3, 8);     // 8
Math.abs(-4);       // 4
Math.pow(2, 10);    // 1024.0
Math.sqrt(16);      // 4.0
```

## Naming

Java uses **camelCase** for variables (`totalPrice`) and **UPPER_CASE** for constants (`MAX_SIZE`).

quiz.q: What does 9 / 2 evaluate to in Java?
quiz.explain: Both are ints, so integer division drops the decimal part.

quiz.q: Which type stores true or false?
quiz.explain: The primitive type is boolean.

quiz.q: What does the final keyword mean on a variable?
options: It is deleted at the end
quiz.explain: A final variable can be assigned only once.

exercise.prompt:
Read two integers, **width** and **height** (separated by whitespace). Print:

Area: A

lessons.title: Input and formatted output
lessons.summary: Read numbers and text with Scanner and format output with printf.

slides.title: Scanner
slides.text: `Scanner` reads from the keyboard (standard input). Import it from `java.util`.
slides.narration: To read what the user types, Java uses a Scanner. You import it at the top of the file, then create one connected to System dot in, the standard input.

slides.title: Reading methods
slides.text:
- `nextInt()`, `nextLong()`, `nextDouble()`
- `next()` one word
- `nextLine()` the rest of the line
- `hasNextInt()` checks first
slides.narration: Scanner has a method for each type. Next int reads a whole number, next reads one word, and next line reads everything up to the end of the line. The has next methods tell you whether more input is waiting.

slides.title: The nextLine trap
slides.text: After `nextInt()`, the newline is still waiting. Call `nextLine()` once to skip it.
slides.narration: A classic beginner bug: you read a number, then call next line and get an empty string. That is because the number was read but the end of the line was not. Call next line once more to throw it away.

slides.title: printf and String.format
slides.text: `%d` integer, `%.2f` 2 decimals, `%s` text, `%n` newline.
slides.narration: For neat output use printf. You write a template with placeholders, then the values. Percent d is for integers, percent point two f shows a decimal with two digits, and percent s is for text.

slides.title: Text blocks and joining
slides.text: Use `+` for simple joins and `printf` when you need formatting.
slides.narration: Joining strings with plus is fine for simple messages. When you need decimals or alignment, printf and String dot format keep the code readable.

quiz.q: Which package contains Scanner?
quiz.explain: Scanner is java.util.Scanner.

quiz.q: What does %.2f print for 3.14159?
quiz.explain: %.2f rounds to two decimals.

quiz.q: Why can nextLine() return an empty string right after nextInt()?
options: The newline after the number has not been consumed yet
quiz.explain: nextInt leaves the line break in the input, so nextLine reads the empty rest of that line.

exercise.title: Average of three
exercise.prompt:
Read **three integers** separated by spaces. Print:

```
Sum: S
Average: A
```

with the average shown with exactly 2 decimals (use `printf` with `%.2f`).

lessons.title: Decisions: if and switch
lessons.summary: Choose what runs with if, else if, else, logical operators and switch.

slides.title: if statements
slides.text: `if (condition) { ... }` runs the block only when the condition is `true`. The condition goes in **brackets**.
slides.narration: An if statement lets your program make a decision. The condition is written inside round brackets and must be a boolean. If it is true, the block in curly braces runs.

slides.title: else if and else
slides.text: Conditions are checked **top to bottom**; only the first true branch runs.
slides.narration: Add else if to test more conditions, and else for everything that is left. Java runs only the first branch whose condition is true and skips the rest.

slides.title: Comparing and combining
slides.narration: Comparison operators give true or false. Combine them with double ampersand for and, double bar for or, and an exclamation mark for not.

slides.title: Comparing Strings
slides.text: Use `a.equals(b)` for text, **not** `==`.
slides.narration: This is one of the most important Java rules. Double equals on strings checks whether they are the very same object in memory, not whether they contain the same text. Always use the equals method to compare strings.

slides.title: switch expressions
slides.text: Modern Java (14+) has arrow-style `switch` that returns a value.
slides.narration: When you compare one value against many fixed options, switch is cleaner than a long chain of if else. The modern arrow form has no fall through and can directly produce a value.

quiz.q: How should you compare two Strings for equal text?
quiz.explain: equals compares content; == compares references.

quiz.q: What does && mean?
quiz.explain: && is logical and.

quiz.q: In an arrow switch, what happens after a matching case runs?
options: It falls through to the next case
quiz.explain: Arrow cases never fall through.

exercise.title: Mini calculator
exercise.prompt:
Read an expression `a op b` where `a` and `b` are integers and `op` is one of `+ - * /` (separated by spaces).

Print the result. For `/` use integer division. If `op` is `/` and `b` is 0, print `error`. Use a `switch`.

lessons.title: Loops
lessons.summary: Repeat code with for, while, do-while, break and continue.

slides.title: The classic for loop
slides.text: `for (start; condition; update)`
slides.narration: Java's for loop has three parts inside the brackets: where to start, when to keep going, and how to move to the next step. It is perfect for counting.

slides.title: while loops
slides.text: `while (condition)` repeats as long as the condition is true.
slides.narration: Use a while loop when you do not know in advance how many rounds you need. The condition is checked before each round.

slides.title: do-while
slides.text: `do { ... } while (cond);` always runs **at least once**.
slides.narration: A do while loop checks its condition at the end, so the body always runs at least one time. It is handy for menus that must be shown before the user chooses.

slides.title: break and continue
slides.text:
- `break` exits the loop
- `continue` jumps to the next round
slides.narration: Break stops the loop immediately. Continue skips the rest of the current round and moves on to the next one.

slides.title: Reading until the end
slides.text: `while (sc.hasNextInt())` reads numbers until input runs out.
slides.narration: Combine a while loop with Scanner's has next int to process every number in the input, no matter how many there are.

quiz.q: How many times does for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) run?
quiz.explain: i takes 0, 1, 2, 3.

quiz.q: Which loop always runs its body at least once?
quiz.explain: do-while checks the condition after the body.

quiz.q: What does continue do?
quiz.explain: continue jumps to the next round of the loop.

lessons.title: Methods
lessons.summary: Write reusable static methods with parameters, return types and overloading.

slides.title: What is a method?
slides.text: A **method** is a named block of code. `main` is one; you can write more.
slides.narration: As programs grow, you split them into methods. Each method does one job and has a name that explains it. You call the method whenever you need that job done.

slides.title: Declaring a method
slides.text: `static returnType name(type param, ...)`
slides.narration: A method declaration lists the return type, the name, and the parameters with their types. For now we use static methods, which belong to the class and can be called directly from main.

slides.title: void methods
slides.text: `void` means the method returns **nothing**. It just does something.
slides.narration: Not every method gives back a value. A method declared void performs an action, like printing, and then simply ends.

slides.title: Overloading
slides.text: Several methods may share a **name** if their **parameter lists differ**.
slides.narration: Java lets you define several methods with the same name, as long as their parameters are different. The compiler picks the right one based on the arguments you pass.

slides.title: Pass by value
slides.text: Java copies arguments into parameters. Changing a parameter does **not** change the caller's variable.
slides.narration: When you pass a number to a method, the method gets its own copy. Changing it inside the method has no effect outside. To get a result back, return it.

quiz.q: What does void mean as a return type?
quiz.explain: void methods do not return a value.

quiz.q: Which pair of methods is valid overloading?
options: int f(int a) and double f(int b)
int f(int a) and int f(int a, int b)
int f(int a) and int g(int a)
quiz.explain: Overloads must differ in parameter list; return type alone is not enough.

quiz.q: After calling addOne(n) where addOne does x++, what is n?
quiz.explain: Primitives are passed by value, so the caller's variable is unchanged.

exercise.title: GCD and LCM
exercise.prompt:
Write two methods: `static long gcd(long a, long b)` (greatest common divisor, use Euclid's algorithm) and `static long lcm(long a, long b)`.

Read two positive integers and print:

```
GCD: G
LCM: L
```

lessons.title: Arrays
lessons.summary: Store fixed-size sequences in arrays, loop over them and use the Arrays helper class.

slides.title: A row of boxes
slides.text:
An **array** holds a fixed number of values of **one type**.

`int[] scores = new int[5];`
slides.narration: An array is a row of boxes, all of the same type. You choose its size when you create it, and that size never changes. New int arrays start filled with zeros.

slides.title: Indexes and length
slides.text: Indexes go from `0` to `length - 1`. Going outside throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`.
slides.narration: The first element is at index zero and the last at length minus one. Notice that length on an array has no brackets. If you use an index outside that range, Java stops with an exception.

slides.title: Looping over arrays
slides.text: Use an index loop when you need positions, and **for-each** when you only need values.
slides.narration: There are two ways to walk through an array. The classic for loop gives you the index. The enhanced for each loop gives you each value directly and is shorter.

slides.title: The Arrays class
slides.text: `java.util.Arrays` has `sort`, `toString`, `fill`, `copyOf`, `equals`.
slides.narration: The Arrays helper class saves you a lot of work. Sort puts the elements in order, toString turns the array into readable text, and copy of makes a resized copy.

slides.title: 2D arrays
slides.text: An array of arrays makes a grid: `int[][] grid = new int[3][4];`
slides.code:
int[][] grid = {{1, 2}, {3, 4}};
System.out.println(grid[1][0]);   // 3
slides.narration: For tables and game boards, use a two dimensional array. The first index chooses the row and the second the column.

quiz.q: What is the last valid index of an array of length 5?
quiz.explain: Indexes run from 0 to length - 1.

quiz.q: How do you get the size of an array a?
quiz.explain: Arrays have a length field, without brackets.

quiz.q: What are the elements of new int[3]?
quiz.explain: Numeric arrays are filled with 0.

exercise.title: Reverse and max
exercise.prompt:
The first number is `n`, followed by `n` integers.

Print two lines:

1. the numbers in **reverse order**, separated by single spaces
2. `Max: M` where M is the largest number

lessons.title: Strings and StringBuilder
lessons.summary: Work with immutable Strings, their methods, chars and the fast StringBuilder.

slides.title: Strings are objects
slides.text: `String` is a class. A string's characters **cannot change** (immutable).
slides.narration: In Java, a String is an object with many useful methods. Strings are immutable: methods like to upper case return a brand new string and leave the original untouched.

slides.title: Essential methods
slides.text: `length()`, `charAt(i)`, `substring(a, b)`, `indexOf(x)`, `contains(x)`, `replace(a, b)`, `trim()`, `split(regex)`
slides.code:
String w = "programming";
System.out.println(w.length());        // 11
System.out.println(w.charAt(0));       // p
System.out.println(w.substring(3, 7)); // gram
System.out.println(w.indexOf("gram")); // 3
slides.narration: These methods cover most everyday text work. Char at gets one character. Substring takes a piece from a start index up to, but not including, an end index. Split cuts the string into an array.

slides.title: char is a number too
slides.text: A `char` like `'a'` is stored as a number. `Character` has `isDigit`, `isLetter`, `toUpperCase`.
slides.narration: A char holds one character in single quotes, and underneath it is just a number. That means you can do arithmetic with it, like moving from a to b. The Character class has helpers for testing characters.

slides.title: StringBuilder
slides.text: Joining with `+` in a loop creates many strings. **StringBuilder** builds one efficiently.
slides.narration: Because strings are immutable, adding to a string inside a big loop creates a new string every time. A StringBuilder is a growable buffer: append to it as much as you like, then call toString once at the end.

slides.title: Comparing strings
slides.text: `equals`, `equalsIgnoreCase`, `compareTo` for alphabetical order.
slides.narration: Remember to compare strings with equals. Compare to tells you the alphabetical order: a negative number means the first string comes before the second.

lessons.notes:
## Creating and joining

```java
String a = "Hello";
String b = a + ", " + "world";       // concatenation
String c = String.join("-", "x", "y", "z");   // "x-y-z"
String d = "ha".repeat(3);           // "hahaha"
```

## Methods

| Method | Example | Result |
|--------|---------|--------|
| `length()` | `"abc".length()` | `3` |
| `charAt(i)` | `"abc".charAt(1)` | `'b'` |
| `substring(a, b)` | `"hello".substring(1, 3)` | `"el"` |
| `indexOf(s)` | `"hello".indexOf("l")` | `2` (or `-1`) |
| `contains(s)` | `"hello".contains("ell")` | `true` |
| `toUpperCase()` | `"hi".toUpperCase()` | `"HI"` |
| `trim()` / `strip()` | `"  x ".strip()` | `"x"` |
| `replace(a, b)` | `"a-b".replace("-", "+")` | `"a+b"` |
| `split(regex)` | `"a b".split(" ")` | `["a", "b"]` |
| `isEmpty()` / `isBlank()` | `"  ".isBlank()` | `true` |

Use `split("\\s+")` to split on any amount of whitespace.

## Characters

```java
for (char ch : text.toCharArray()) {
    if (Character.isLetter(ch)) letters++;
}
int digit = '7' - '0';    // 7
```

## StringBuilder

```java
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("abc");
sb.append("def");      // abcdef
sb.insert(0, ">");     // >abcdef
sb.reverse();          // fedcba>
String result = sb.toString();
```

## Comparing

```java
"apple".equals("apple");           // true
"Apple".equalsIgnoreCase("apple"); // true
"apple".compareTo("banana") < 0;   // true, apple comes first
```

## Converting

```java
int n = Integer.parseInt("42");
double x = Double.parseDouble("2.5");
String s = String.valueOf(99);
```

quiz.q: What is "hello".substring(1, 4)?
quiz.explain: From index 1 up to but not including 4: e, l, l.

quiz.q: Why use StringBuilder in a loop?
options: It avoids creating a new String on every append
quiz.explain: StringBuilder is mutable, so appending is cheap.

quiz.q: What does "abc".charAt(2) return?
quiz.explain: Index 2 is the third character, the char 'c'.

exercise.title: Caesar cipher
exercise.prompt:
The first line is an integer shift `k` (0 to 25). The second line is a message.

Shift every **letter** forward by `k` places in the alphabet, wrapping from `z` to `a`. Keep upper and lower case. Leave other characters unchanged. Print the result.

lessons.title: ArrayList and HashMap
lessons.summary: Use growable lists and key-value maps from the collections library.

slides.title: Lists that grow
slides.text: `ArrayList<T>` is like an array that **resizes** itself.
slides.narration: Arrays have a fixed size, which is often inconvenient. An ArrayList grows and shrinks as you add and remove elements. The type in angle brackets says what it holds.

slides.title: List methods
slides.text: `add`, `get(i)`, `set(i, x)`, `remove`, `contains`, `size`, `isEmpty`
slides.narration: You add with add, read with get, replace with set, and delete with remove. Size tells you how many elements there are. Lists print nicely with println.

slides.title: Wrapper types
slides.text: Collections hold **objects**, so use `Integer`, `Double`, `Character` instead of `int`, `double`, `char`.
slides.narration: Collections can only store objects, not primitives. Java provides wrapper classes like Integer and Double, and converts between them automatically. This is called autoboxing.

slides.title: HashMap
slides.text: `HashMap<K, V>` maps **keys** to **values** for fast lookup.
slides.narration: A map stores pairs of keys and values. You put a pair in, and later get the value back by its key, very quickly. Each key appears only once.

slides.title: Counting with a map
slides.text: `map.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum)` adds one to a counter.
slides.narration: Counting things is the classic use of a map. Merge puts one for a new key, or adds one to the existing value. Use a TreeMap instead of a HashMap when you want the keys sorted.

quiz.q: Which can grow after it is created?
quiz.explain: ArrayList resizes automatically.

quiz.q: Why write List<Integer> instead of List<int>?
options: It is a style choice only
quiz.explain: Generic types require object types, so the wrapper Integer is used.

quiz.q: Which map keeps keys sorted?
quiz.explain: TreeMap stores keys in sorted order.

exercise.title: Word frequency
exercise.prompt:
Read one line of lowercase words separated by spaces.

Print each distinct word and its count as `word count`, one per line, sorted **alphabetically**.

lessons.title: Classes and objects
lessons.summary: Design your own types with fields, constructors, methods and encapsulation.

slides.title: Classes are blueprints
slides.text: A **class** describes data (fields) and behavior (methods). An **object** is one instance created with `new`.
slides.narration: Java is built around classes. A class is a blueprint that says what data each object holds and what it can do. You create real objects from it with the keyword new.

slides.title: Fields and a constructor
slides.text: The **constructor** has the class name and no return type. `this` refers to the current object.
slides.narration: Fields store each object's data. The constructor runs when you write new, and sets up those fields. The keyword this means the object being built, which helps when a parameter has the same name as a field.

slides.title: Instance methods
slides.text: Methods **without** `static` work on one object and can use its fields.
slides.narration: Until now our methods were static. Instance methods belong to each object and can read and change that object's fields. You call them with a dot on the object.

slides.title: Encapsulation
slides.text: Make fields `private`. Expose safe `public` methods (getters, setters, actions).
slides.narration: Professional Java hides an object's data. Fields are private, so only the class itself can change them. Other code uses public methods, which can check that every change is valid.

slides.title: toString and records
slides.text: Override `toString()` for readable printing. For simple data, a `record` writes everything for you.
slides.narration: If you override toString, println shows your object nicely. And since Java 16, a record is a compact way to declare a class that just carries data. It automatically gets a constructor, getters, equals and toString.

quiz.q: What keyword creates an object?
quiz.explain: new allocates and constructs an object.

quiz.q: What does this refer to inside a method?
quiz.explain: this is the object the method was called on.

quiz.q: Why make fields private?
options: So only the class controls changes to its data
quiz.explain: Encapsulation protects an object's data from invalid changes.

lessons.title: Inheritance and polymorphism
lessons.summary: Extend classes, override methods, use abstract classes and dynamic dispatch.

slides.title: extends
slides.text: `class Dog extends Animal` makes Dog a **subclass** that inherits Animal's fields and methods.
slides.narration: Inheritance lets one class build on another. The subclass gets everything from its superclass and can add more. In Java a class can extend only one other class.

slides.title: super
slides.text: `super(...)` calls the parent constructor. `super.method()` calls the parent's version.
slides.narration: A subclass constructor must first build the parent part of the object, using super with the right arguments. Inside methods, super dot method calls the parent's implementation.

slides.title: Overriding
slides.text: Redefine a parent method with the **same signature**. Mark it `@Override`.
slides.narration: To change behavior, a subclass overrides a method by writing one with the same name and parameters. The at Override annotation asks the compiler to check that you really are overriding something, which catches typos.

slides.title: Polymorphism
slides.text: A variable of the **parent type** can hold any subclass object. The **actual** object's method runs.
slides.narration: This is the heart of object oriented design. You can store a Dog or a Cat in a variable of type Animal. When you call sound, Java looks at the real object and runs its own version. This is called dynamic dispatch.

slides.title: Abstract classes
slides.text: An `abstract` class cannot be created directly. `abstract` methods **must** be implemented by subclasses.
slides.narration: Sometimes the parent is only a general idea, like Shape. Mark it abstract so nobody can create a plain Shape, and declare abstract methods that every concrete subclass must provide.

quiz.q: Which keyword makes a subclass?
quiz.explain: class B extends A.

quiz.q: What does @Override do?
options: Asks the compiler to check the method really overrides a parent method
quiz.explain: It is a safety check against typos in method signatures.

quiz.q: Animal a = new Dog(); a.sound(); Which sound() runs?
quiz.explain: Dynamic dispatch runs the method of the actual object, a Dog.

lessons.title: Exceptions
lessons.summary: Handle runtime errors with try, catch, finally, throw and custom exceptions.

slides.title: When things go wrong
slides.text: An **exception** is an object describing an error that happened while the program ran.
slides.narration: Programs meet unexpected situations: text where a number was expected, division by zero, or an index outside an array. Java represents these as exception objects. If nobody catches one, the program stops and prints a stack trace.

slides.title: try and catch
slides.text: Put risky code in `try`; handle specific errors in `catch` blocks.
slides.narration: Wrap code that might fail in a try block. If an exception is thrown, Java jumps to the first catch block whose type matches, and then continues after the whole try statement.

slides.title: finally
slides.text: `finally` runs **always**, error or not. Perfect for cleanup.
slides.narration: A finally block runs whether the try succeeded, failed, or even returned early. It is used to release resources. For files and connections, modern Java prefers try with resources, which closes them automatically.

slides.title: throw and throws
slides.text: `throw new X(...)` signals an error. Checked exceptions must be declared with `throws`.
slides.narration: You can throw your own exceptions when a method receives bad input. Java has two kinds: unchecked exceptions, like IllegalArgumentException, and checked ones, like IOException, which the compiler forces you to catch or declare.

slides.title: Custom exceptions
slides.text: Extend `Exception` (checked) or `RuntimeException` (unchecked).
slides.narration: For errors that belong to your own program, create your own exception class. A clear name like InsufficientFundsException tells readers exactly what went wrong.

quiz.q: Which exception does Integer.parseInt("hi") throw?
quiz.explain: The text is not a valid number, so NumberFormatException is thrown.

quiz.q: When does a finally block run?
quiz.explain: finally always runs.

quiz.q: Which is a checked exception?
quiz.explain: IOException is checked; the others extend RuntimeException.

lessons.title: Interfaces
lessons.summary: Define contracts with interfaces, implement several of them and use default methods.

slides.title: A contract
slides.text: An **interface** lists methods a class promises to provide, without saying how.
slides.narration: An interface is a contract. It names the methods a class must have, but not how they work. Any class that implements the interface promises to provide all of them.

slides.title: implements
slides.text: `class Circle implements Shape` must implement every abstract method.
slides.narration: A class signs the contract with the keyword implements. The compiler then checks that every method of the interface is really there. Interface methods are public, so the implementations must be public too.

slides.title: Many interfaces
slides.text: A class extends **one** class but can implement **many** interfaces.
slides.narration: Java allows only one superclass, but a class may implement as many interfaces as it needs. This lets one object play several roles, for example being both Comparable and Printable.

slides.title: Default and static methods
slides.text: Interfaces may contain `default` methods with a body, and `static` helpers.
slides.narration: Since Java 8, an interface can include default methods, which give every implementing class a ready made behavior that it may override. Static methods in an interface are utility functions related to it.

slides.title: Functional interfaces and lambdas
slides.text: An interface with **one** abstract method can be implemented by a **lambda**: `x -> x * 2`.
slides.narration: When an interface has exactly one abstract method, you can implement it with a short lambda expression instead of a whole class. Java's Comparator, Runnable and Function are all functional interfaces.

quiz.q: How many interfaces can a class implement?
quiz.explain: A class can implement multiple interfaces.

quiz.q: What is a functional interface?
options: An interface with exactly one abstract method
quiz.explain: One abstract method means it can be implemented with a lambda.

quiz.q: What keyword lets an interface method have a body for all implementers?
quiz.explain: default methods provide a shared implementation.

lessons.title: Generics
lessons.summary: Write type-safe classes and methods that work with any type using <T>.

slides.title: Why generics?
slides.text: Generics let one class or method work with **many types** while the compiler still checks them.
slides.narration: Without generics you would need a separate box class for integers, strings and every other type, or lose type safety. Generics let you write the code once with a type parameter, and the compiler fills in the real type.

slides.title: A generic class
slides.text: `class Box<T>`: `T` is a **type parameter**, replaced when you use it.
slides.narration: Write the type parameter in angle brackets after the class name. Inside the class, T stands for whatever type the user chooses. When you write Box of String, every T becomes String.

slides.title: Generic methods
slides.text: Put `<T>` before the return type: `static <T> T first(List<T> list)`.
slides.narration: Methods can have their own type parameters too. They go in angle brackets right before the return type. Java usually infers the type from the arguments you pass.

slides.title: Bounded types
slides.text: `<T extends Comparable<T>>` means T must be comparable, so you can call `compareTo`.
slides.narration: Sometimes your code needs the type to have certain abilities. A bound says T must extend or implement something, so inside the method you can safely use that ability, such as compare to.

slides.title: Wildcards
slides.text: `List<? extends Number>` reads numbers of any subtype. `? super T` accepts writes of T.
slides.narration: Wildcards make methods more flexible. A list of question mark extends Number can be a list of integers or of doubles, which is great for reading. A simple rule: producer extends, consumer super.

quiz.q: Which is NOT allowed?
quiz.explain: Type arguments must be reference types, not primitives.

quiz.q: What does <T extends Comparable<T>> guarantee?
options: Values of T can be compared with compareTo
quiz.explain: The bound ensures compareTo is available.

quiz.q: Where is the type parameter of a generic method written?
quiz.explain: For example: static <T> T first(List<T> list).

lessons.title: The Collections Framework
lessons.summary: Choose the right collection: List, Set, Map, Queue and Deque, and know their costs.

slides.title: A family of interfaces
slides.text:
- `List`: ordered, duplicates OK
- `Set`: unique items
- `Map`: key to value
- `Queue` / `Deque`: process in order
slides.narration: The Java Collections Framework is a set of interfaces with several implementations each. Choosing the right one makes your program simpler and faster. Think about what you need: order, uniqueness, lookup by key, or first in first out.

slides.title: Sets
slides.text: `HashSet` (fast, no order), `LinkedHashSet` (insertion order), `TreeSet` (sorted).
slides.narration: A set keeps each element only once. Hash set is the fastest. Linked hash set remembers insertion order. Tree set keeps elements sorted and can find the next bigger or smaller element.

slides.title: Maps
slides.text: `HashMap`, `LinkedHashMap`, `TreeMap`. Useful: `getOrDefault`, `merge`, `computeIfAbsent`.
slides.narration: Maps come in the same three flavors as sets. The compute if absent method is perfect for grouping: it creates an empty list the first time a key appears and then you add to it.

slides.title: Queues and deques
slides.text: `ArrayDeque` is a fast queue **and** stack. `PriorityQueue` always gives the smallest first.
slides.narration: A queue processes items in arrival order: offer adds at the back, poll takes from the front. Array deque also works as a stack with push and pop. A priority queue always hands out the smallest element first.

slides.title: Big-O at a glance
slides.text:
- `ArrayList.get`: O(1)
- `HashMap/HashSet` lookup: O(1) average
- `TreeMap/TreeSet`: O(log n)
- `List.contains`: O(n)
slides.narration: Different collections have different costs. Looking something up in a hash map is almost instant, while searching a list checks every element. For big data, picking the right structure matters more than anything else.

lessons.notes:
## Choosing a collection

| Need | Use |
|------|-----|
| ordered list, index access | `ArrayList` |
| unique items, fast lookup | `HashSet` |
| unique items, sorted | `TreeSet` |
| key-value, fast | `HashMap` |
| key-value, sorted keys | `TreeMap` |
| keep insertion order | `LinkedHashMap` / `LinkedHashSet` |
| FIFO queue or stack | `ArrayDeque` |
| always smallest first | `PriorityQueue` |

## Immutable collections

```java
List<String> days = List.of("Mon", "Tue");
Set<Integer> primes = Set.of(2, 3, 5);
Map<String, Integer> ages = Map.of("Ana", 15, "Leo", 17);
```

These cannot be modified; `add` throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. Copy into `new ArrayList<>(days)` to change it.

## The Collections utility class

```java
Collections.sort(list);
Collections.reverse(list);
Collections.max(list);
Collections.frequency(list, "x");
Collections.unmodifiableList(list);
```

## TreeMap navigation

```java
TreeMap<Integer, String> grades = new TreeMap<>(Map.of(90, "A", 80, "B", 70, "C"));
grades.floorEntry(85).getValue();   // "B"
grades.firstKey();                  // 70
```

## Iterating safely

Removing from a collection inside a for-each throws `ConcurrentModificationException`. Use `removeIf`:

```java
list.removeIf(x -> x < 0);
```

## equals and hashCode

Objects used as `HashMap` keys or in a `HashSet` must implement `equals` and `hashCode` consistently. Records do this automatically.

## PriorityQueue with a comparator

```java
PriorityQueue<String> pq = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparing(String::length));
```

quiz.q: Which collection removes duplicates and keeps items sorted?
quiz.explain: TreeSet is a sorted set.

quiz.q: What does PriorityQueue.poll() return?
options: The smallest element by its ordering
quiz.explain: A priority queue always removes the smallest element first.

quiz.q: Which is O(1) on average?
quiz.explain: Hash lookups take constant time on average.

lessons.title: Lambdas and streams
lessons.summary: Process collections declaratively with lambdas, method references and the Stream API.

slides.title: Say what, not how
slides.text: A **stream** is a pipeline: source, then operations, then a result.
slides.narration: Streams let you describe what you want from a collection instead of writing loops step by step. You take a source, chain operations like filter and map, and finish with a terminal operation that produces the result.

slides.title: filter, map, collect
slides.text:
- `filter` keeps matching items
- `map` transforms each item
- `toList()` collects the result
slides.narration: Filter keeps only the elements that pass a test. Map turns each element into something else. Finally toList gathers the results into a new list. The original list is never changed.

slides.title: Method references
slides.text: `String::toUpperCase` is short for `s -> s.toUpperCase()`.
slides.narration: When a lambda just calls one existing method, you can write a method reference instead, with two colons. It is shorter and often easier to read.

slides.title: Reducing to one value
slides.text: `count`, `sum`, `average`, `max`, `reduce`. Use `mapToInt` for number streams.
slides.narration: Terminal operations can boil a stream down to a single value. Number streams such as int stream have sum, average, and summary statistics built in.

slides.title: Grouping
slides.text: `Collectors.groupingBy` builds a `Map` from a stream, like SQL GROUP BY.
slides.narration: The collectors class holds powerful recipes. Grouping by splits elements into groups by a key, and you can count or sum each group, just like group by in a database query.

slides.title: Laziness and Optional
slides.text: Intermediate steps run only when a **terminal** operation is called. `findFirst` and `max` return an `Optional`.
slides.narration: Streams are lazy: nothing happens until a terminal operation asks for the result. Some results might not exist, like the maximum of an empty list, so Java wraps them in an Optional, which forces you to handle the empty case.

lessons.notes:
## Lambdas

```java
Function<Integer, Integer> square = x -> x * x;
Predicate<String> isEmpty = s -> s.isEmpty();
BiFunction<Integer, Integer, Integer> add = (a, b) -> a + b;
Runnable hello = () -> System.out.println("hi");
```

## Building a stream pipeline

```java
List<String> result = words.stream()      // source
    .filter(w -> w.length() > 3)          // intermediate
    .map(String::toLowerCase)             // intermediate
    .sorted()                             // intermediate
    .distinct()                           // intermediate
    .toList();                            // terminal
```

## Sources

`list.stream()`, `Arrays.stream(arr)`, `Stream.of(a, b, c)`, `IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 10)`.

## Common operations

| Intermediate | Terminal |
|--------------|----------|
| `filter` | `toList`, `collect` |
| `map`, `mapToInt` | `forEach` |
| `sorted`, `distinct` | `count`, `sum`, `average` |
| `limit`, `skip` | `min`, `max`, `findFirst` |
| `flatMap` | `anyMatch`, `allMatch`, `reduce` |

## Collectors

```java
import java.util.stream.Collectors;

Map<Boolean, List<Integer>> parts = nums.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.partitioningBy(n -> n % 2 == 0));
String csv = words.stream().collect(Collectors.joining(", "));
Map<String, Integer> totals = sales.stream()
    .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Sale::region, TreeMap::new,
             Collectors.summingInt(Sale::amount)));
```

## Optional

```java
Optional<String> longest = words.stream().max(Comparator.comparing(String::length));
System.out.println(longest.orElse("none"));
```

## Tips

- Streams are single-use: create a new one for each pipeline.
- Keep lambdas short and free of side effects.
- A clear loop is still fine. Use streams when they make the intent clearer.

## You made it

You now know modern Java from `main` to streams. Next steps: build a small project, learn JUnit for tests, and explore records, sealed types and pattern matching further.

quiz.q: What does filter do in a stream?
options: Keeps elements that match a condition
quiz.explain: filter keeps only elements for which the predicate is true.

quiz.q: When do intermediate operations actually run?
options: When a terminal operation is called
quiz.explain: Streams are lazy.

quiz.q: What is String::length?
quiz.explain: It is a method reference, short for s -> s.length().
